video.title: Why Your Wrist Hurts, and How to Fix It

classification.reason: Coach provides actionable execution cues instructing players to hit during the early stretch-release phase and maintain an elastic support role without actively flexing the wrist.

problem.title_as_question: Why does your wrist hurt when hitting a forehand, and how can you fix it?
problem.definition: Players develop wrist pain when attempting to generate topspin because they mistake fast post-contact rotational racket speed for forward driving speed, causing them to contact late and actively flex the wrist.
problem.target_player: tennis players experiencing wrist pain or fatigue on their forehand

symptoms.description: Wrist and hand muscles fatigue repeatedly and eventually develop pain.
Ball lacks penetration and does not go anywhere when attempting to hit during the fast-feeling follow-through.
Contact occurs late in the swing during the windshield wiper roll rather than right after the lag slot.

causes.statement: Small muscles of the wrist and hand are forced into active flexion to drive the heavy racket instead of acting as an elastic stretch-and-release conduit.
Players make contact too late in the swing after the back-to-front forward momentum has already dissipated.
The player's brain perceives high rotational racket head speed during the follow-through and mistakes it for the hitting zone.
Forward driving racket head speed peaks and finishes early at release, while subsequent swing speed is purely rotational roll from pronation and internal rotation.

angles.summary: Coach breaks down slow-motion frames of Roger Federer to show the precise timing of wrist lag, contact, and follow-through roll.
Back-to-front driving speed maxes out between lag and contact, whereas follow-through speed is purely rotational pronation and internal rotation.
Players wrongly think the windshield wiper is the hitting action, ignoring that 90% of the wiper happens after contact as a follow-through.
The hitting slot feels like an early elastic stretch-and-release throw rather than an active wrist flex through the ball.

solutions.summary: Cue yourself that the true hitting slot is earlier in the stretch-release elastic feeling than it intuitively seems.
Keep the wrist and hand muscles purely in an elastic support-and-release role, transferring momentum from large muscles without actively flexing.
Focus on hitting solely during the early stretch-release phase and never try to drive the ball during the late rolling follow-through phase.
